summary: Alpena Light on the Thunder Bay River breakwater: a sixth-order light from 1877, burned in 1888, rebuilt, and a 1914 skeletal tower now owned by a conservancy.

lens.where: Removed around 1987; LighthouseFriends says it is at Grand Traverse Lighthouse. USLHS dates the fourth-order lens to 1914; LighthouseFriends gives its service from 1888.

structures.note: Open frame tower on a timber crib; focal plane 44.5 ft (13.6 m) above the base (LighthouseFriends)
Second tower, 18 ft square at the base, 50 ft high, after the 1888 fire
Black skeletal tower on a concrete pier; 44 ft from base to lantern centre (USLHS). Cast iron per USLHS.
Six-room frame dwelling on a city lot bought June 1877
Brick oil house, built thirty feet from the dwelling

access.note: USLHS: not open to the public. LighthouseFriends: tower closed; the breakwater walkway gives a view.

facts.agency: Michigan Lighthouse Conservancy (owner, awarded 2013, per LighthouseFriends). The station record lists the U.S. Coast Guard as agency; the Coast Guard declared the station excess in 2011.
registers: NRHP 06000197 (listing date from the station record; nomination not digitised, not checked)

events.note: Congress appropriates $10,000 for a light at Trowbridge Point; the Board later moves the site to the river mouth
Congress approves the site change to the river mouth on 20 July 1868
Congress provides $20,000 for the light, on condition that tolls on the river be abolished
Temporary light on a cluster of piles at the river mouth (September 1875 per LighthouseFriends; first shown 25 October 1875 per Pepper)
Crib and open frame tower completed in July 1877 on the north pier
Fixed red light from a sixth-order Fresnel shown from 18 August 1877
Fire of 12 July 1888 destroys the lighthouse, its sixth-order lens, the lantern and the stores in the tower
Second tower, eighteen feet square at the base and fifty feet high, on a new crib with a lantern from North Point, Milwaukee
Fourth-order lens from Two Harbors put into operation 1 October 1888
Sixth-order lens replaces the fourth-order lens in April 1889
Fog bell sounded for the first time on 20 March 1891
Electric siren replaces the fog bell on 28 June 1902 (LighthouseFriends; the USLHS record and the 1920 Bulletin give 1920)
Third light: black skeletal tower on a concrete pier, first exhibited 26 June 1914
Fixed red changed to a white light alternately on and off for one second, 22 April 1918; the Bulletin says occulting white
Electric siren fog signal established, per the 1920 Bulletin and the USLHS record
Compressed-air fog signal replaces the siren
Tower painted red
Fourth-order lens removed around 1987; now at Grand Traverse Lighthouse
Declared excess to the needs of the Coast Guard; made available under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act of 2000
Awarded to the Michigan Lighthouse Conservancy

corrections.why: The skeletal tower in the station record is dated 1875 with a 10.0 m height. LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record date the skeletal tower to 1914 and give 44 ft (13.4 m) from base to lantern centre. The 1875 date belongs to the temporary light; the first permanent tower was 1877.
LighthouseFriends says the Conservancy was awarded the lighthouse in 2013 and owns it. The Coast Guard declared it excess in 2011.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station record gives 1875 (Rowlett) and 1877 (USLHS). A temporary light on piles was shown from 1875; the permanent light's first night was 18 August 1877, per the Board's notice in the Alpena Weekly Argus. The story uses 1877 for the permanent light and calls the 1875 light temporary.
LighthouseFriends dates an electric siren to 1902. The USLHS record and the 1920 Bulletin give an electric siren in 1920. Not resolved; the story gives both.

notes_for_editor: (0) No woman keeper, or family member who kept the light in her own right, appears in the USLHS roster or in the sources read for this station. (1) The Board's annual reports for 1875 to 1890, 1898, 1902 and 1914 are not in the local corpus. The 1877 first light rests on the Argus notice, which is primary. The 1888 second tower, the 1914 third light and the 1902 siren rest on LighthouseFriends, with Pepper for 1875 to 1888. (2) Temporary light: LighthouseFriends says placed in September 1875; Pepper says first shown the night of 25 October 1875. The story reports both. (3) Fog signal: LighthouseFriends says an electric siren in 1902; the USLHS record and the 1920 Bulletin say electric siren in 1920. Unresolved. (4) Lens: the USLHS record gives a fourth-order lens installed in 1914. LighthouseFriends gives a fourth-order lens from Two Harbors in service at the 1888 tower from 1 October 1888 and removed around 1987, without a 1914 install date. The story avoids the 1914 lens claim. (5) The 1918 Bulletin entry is badly OCR'd ('iixecl red'). The story uses LighthouseFriends for 'fixed red' and the Bulletin only for 'occulting white'. (6) The NRHP nomination (06000197) is not digitised; the fetch returns the placeholder. The 2006 listing date from the station record is unverified. (7) Terry Pepper's history is used with attribution; the alpenalighthouse.org history repeats Pepper with permission and is not cited separately. (8) Name collision: an 1880 steamer named Alpena was lost on Lake Michigan (1881 LSS report). It is not this light, and the story does not use it. (9) No rescue or wreck tied to this light was found in the sources read. The LSS narratives mention Alpena as a port and the Thunder Bay Island station, which is a different station. (10) Burzlaff's earlier stations are from LighthouseFriends and are not verified in primary records. Only Raspberry Island has a date. (11) Living or recent keepers and Coast Guard crew (roster lines after about 1960) appear only as the roster prints them; the story names none of them. (12) The record's characteristic and range fields were not verified. Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: (a) Wallace's end date: the USLHS roster ends his service in 1915; Pepper says he resigned on 7 June 1920 after 31 years. The story gives both and says the roster has no keeper between 1915 and 1920. The roster line keeps the USLHS dates. (b) The 1918 characteristic change: LighthouseFriends dates it 22 April 1918 (one second on, one off); Pepper dates the change to occulting white to 28 June 1918. The Bulletin's 1918 entry (OCR: 'iixecl red') gives the change to occulting white without a day; the story gives LighthouseFriends' and Pepper's dates. (c) Fog signal: LighthouseFriends 1902; USLHS, the 1920 Bulletin and Pepper 1920 (three weeks after Burzlaff's arrival). Stated as a disagreement. (d) Fourth-order lens: Pepper places it in the 1914 tower (returned to Detroit storage in 1889); USLHS dates the original 1914 lens; LighthouseFriends says it came out of the tower around 1987. (e) The 1877 Argus notice gives the focal plane as 53 feet above the lake level; LighthouseFriends gives 44.5 feet from the base to the focal plane. The story uses LighthouseFriends' figure with its reference. (f) The story no longer says 'no rescues were found in the sources read'; that statement stays here (note 9).
